procedural_history.originating_court: Police Station Mirzapur, District Saharanpur (where FIR No. 224 of 2022 was registered)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 17.10.2022 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in CRLMWP No. 15174 of 2022.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellants filed a Criminal Miscellaneous Writ Petition (CRLMWP No. 15174 of 2022) before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad seeking to quash F.I.R. dated 19.09.2022, registered as Case Crime No. 0224 of 2022, under sections 395, 504, 506, 323 I.P.C., Police Station Mirzapur, District Saharanpur. The High Court dismissed the petition, allowing the petitioners to apply for anticipatory bail/bail before the competent court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Feeling aggrieved and dissatisfied with the High Court's order refusing to quash the FIR, the appellants approached the Supreme Court with a Special Leave Petition (converted into Criminal Appeal No. 2340 of 2023). The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and effectively quashed the FIR, finding the case to be concocted and an abuse of the process of law.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad is hereby set aside.
The criminal proceedings arising from FIR No. 224 of 2022 dated 19.09.2022 registered at Police Station Mirzapur, Saharanpur, State of U.P. are hereby quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the case falls within the parameters laid down for quashing the FIR, particularly those established in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal.

facts: An FIR was filed against the appellants for assault and dacoity (Sections 395, 504, 506, 323 IPC) over a land dispute.
The FIR was lodged more than one year after the alleged incident, and it failed to specify the date and time the incident occurred.
The High Court had previously refused to quash the FIR, stating that it prima facie revealed a cognizable offense.
The Supreme Court, upon review, found the informant's entire case to appear "concocted and fabricated" on its face.
law: The Supreme Court relied on the parameters established in *State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal* for quashing an FIR.
When an accused claims proceedings are frivolous, vexatious, or instituted with an ulterior motive, a court has a duty to look beyond the mere averments in the FIR.
The court must examine other attending circumstances and, if necessary, "read in between the lines."
While a delay in filing an FIR is not, by itself, a ground for quashing, it can be a valid ground when combined with other circumstances that render the prosecution's case "inherently improbable."
application: The Court determined that its duty was not just to read the FIR but to look more closely at the overall circumstances, as the case appeared frivolous.
It identified the delay of over one year in lodging the FIR as a significant attending circumstance.

This delay, combined with the vagueness of the allegations (specifically the failure to mention the date and time of the incident), rendered the entire case put up by the prosecution "inherently improbable."
The Court reasoned that such vague allegations, lodged after a significant delay, make it impossible for an accused to properly defend themselves.
Based on these factors, the Court concluded that the allegations did not prima facie constitute an offense and that the proceedings were manifestly frivolous and vexatious.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the case fell within the parameters for quashing an FIR as laid down in *Bhajan Lal*. It found that the significant and unexplained delay, coupled with the vague allegations, made the informant's story inherently improbable, concocted, and fabricated, thus justifying the quashing of the criminal proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the plain reading of the FIR discloses commission of the offence of dacoity punishable u/s. 395 IPC.

facts: An FIR was registered against the appellant and co-accused for offences including dacoity under Section 395 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The FIR alleged that the informant and his brother went to the appellant's house to settle a land dispute.
While at the house, the appellant and co-accused allegedly assaulted the informant and his brother and forcibly took Rs. 2 lakh from the informant's pocket.
law: The Court analyzed the definition of "dacoity" under Section 391 of the IPC, which requires five or more persons conjointly committing or attempting to commit a "robbery".
It also examined the definition of "robbery" under Section 390 of the IPC.
For theft to be considered robbery, any violence or threat of violence must be used "for that end," meaning for the specific purpose of committing the theft or carrying away the stolen property.
application: The Court determined that the essential ingredients of dacoity were not present in the allegations.
It reasoned that the informant and his brother had gone to the appellant's house voluntarily to settle a pre-existing land dispute.

The alleged assault and taking of money occurred during this meeting. The Court found that the violence was not used "for that end" (i.e., for the purpose of committing the theft). Instead, the entire incident stemmed from the land dispute.
The Court criticized the prosecution for "blindfoldedly" and incorrectly applying the charge of dacoity without understanding its legal requirements.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a plain reading of the FIR did not disclose the commission of the offence of dacoity under Section 395 of the IPC because a key ingredient of robbery—that the violence was used for the purpose of committing the theft—was not met.

issue.issue_text: Whether any case of criminal intimidation punishable u/ss. 504 and 506(2) IPC is made out from the allegations in the FIR.

facts: The informant filed an FIR alleging that while visiting the appellant's house to settle a land dispute, the accused used abusive language, assaulted the informant and his brother, stole money, and forcibly obtained their signatures on a blank paper.
The FIR was registered under several sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), including Section 504 (intentional insult) and Section 506 (criminal intimidation).
law: To establish an offense of criminal intimidation under Section 506 IPC, it must be proven that the accused had an intention to cause alarm to the complainant.

To establish an offense under Section 504 IPC, there must be an act of intentional insult. If this act involves abusive words, the specific words used must be known to determine if they legally constitute an intentional insult.
application: The Court analyzed the allegations for each section separately.
For Section 504, the Court noted that the FIR only stated that "abusive language was used" but did not specify what words were actually spoken.
The Court reasoned that without knowing the specific words, it was impossible to determine whether the essential element of "intentional insult" was present.
For Section 506, the Court initially observed that a prima facie case *might* be disclosed based on the overall incident.
However, when concluding on the issue as a whole, the Court found that a case under both sections was not made out, primarily due to the fatal deficiency in the allegation for Section 504.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the allegations in the FIR did not make out a case of criminal intimidation under Sections 504 and 506 of the IPC. The charge under Section 504 failed because the FIR did not state the specific abusive words used, making it impossible to establish the necessary element of 'intentional insult'.

issue.issue_text: Whether the allegations levelled in the FIR inspire any confidence considering the delay of one year in lodging the FIR.

facts: The FIR was filed in 2022 for an offense that allegedly occurred sometime in 2021, a delay of over one year.
The FIR did not specify the exact date or time of the alleged incident.
The person filing the FIR (the first informant) did not provide any plausible or convincing explanation for this inordinate delay.
The court found the allegations in the FIR to be "too vague and general."
law: The Court clarified that a delay in filing an FIR, by itself, is not a sufficient ground to quash it.
However, a delay combined with other "attending circumstances" that make the prosecution's case "inherently improbable" can be a valid reason for quashing the FIR.
application: The Court applied its legal principle by looking at the delay in conjunction with other factors.
It identified the "attending circumstances" in this case as the lack of specific details (date and time) and the absence of any reasonable explanation for the one-year delay.
The Court reasoned that this combination of factors severely prejudices the accused, as it becomes impossible for them to defend themselves against such vague allegations made after a long time.
Furthermore, the delay hampered the investigation, making it unlikely that key evidence, such as the allegedly stolen money or a forcedly signed document, could be recovered to support the claims.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the allegations in the FIR did not inspire confidence. While delay alone is not enough to dismiss a case, the unexplained delay of over a year, combined with the vagueness of the allegations and the lack of specific details, rendered the entire case "inherently improbable" and unfair to the accused, thus justifying the quashing of the FIR.

issue.issue_text: Whether the criminal antecedents of an accused can be the sole consideration to decline the quashing of criminal proceedings.

facts: The State, represented by the Additional Advocate General, argued against quashing the criminal proceedings against the appellants.
The State's primary argument was based on the appellants' "gross criminal antecedents," submitting a chart that portrayed them as "history sheeters and hardened criminals."
law: An accused's criminal antecedents cannot be the sole consideration for a court to refuse to quash criminal proceedings.

An accused person, regardless of their past, has a legitimate right to argue that if the First Information Report (FIR) fails to disclose the commission of any offense, the proceedings should be quashed.
Article 21 of the Constitution includes the right not to be disturbed by legal proceedings without sufficient grounds.
The State has a dual duty: to ensure crimes are punished and to protect its citizens from unnecessary harassment and injustice.
Courts must balance the power of law enforcement with the protection of citizens.
application: The Court acknowledged the State's submission regarding the appellants' extensive criminal history.
However, the Court reasoned that this history is not the primary factor when deciding whether to quash a case. The fundamental question is whether the FIR itself makes out a case against the accused.

The Court emphasized that initiating a prosecution has severe and harsh consequences for an individual. Therefore, even a person with a bad record is entitled to protection from baseless or harassing legal proceedings.
Allowing criminal history to be the sole reason to continue a case would undermine the accused's right to challenge proceedings that are fundamentally flawed, such as when the FIR discloses no crime.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the criminal antecedents of an accused cannot be the sole reason to refuse to quash criminal proceedings. A court must first examine the FIR to determine if it discloses the commission of an offense; if it does not, the proceedings should be quashed, regardless of the accused's past record.

cases.case_name: Sheonandan Paswan v. State of Bihar
cases.principle: A penal statute must be strictly construed. The Court must see that the thing charged is an offence within the plain meaning of the words used and must not strain the words.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When construing a penal statute, the court must ensure that the charged offense falls within the plain meaning of the words used in the statute and must not strain the meaning of those words.
obiter: The authority of the court exists for the advancement of justice, and the court has the power to prevent any abuse of that authority which would result in injustice.
If a statute is to be strictly construed, nothing should be included within its scope that does not come clearly within the meaning of the language used.
The rule of strict construction means that everything shall be excluded from a statute's operation which does not clearly come within the scope of the language used.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the criminal proceedings were an abuse of the process of law and that the allegations in the FIR did not constitute the offences alleged, particularly dacoity under Section 395 of the IPC. The court found that the case fell squarely within the parameters for quashing an FIR as established in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, specifically categories 1 (allegations do not constitute an offence), 5 (allegations are inherently improbable), and 7 (proceedings are maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive).
legal_tests_applied: The parameters for quashing an FIR laid down in State of Haryana and others vs. Bhajan Lal and others, 1992 Supp. (1) SCC 335. The court specifically found the present case falls within parameters 1, 5, and 7 of this test.
policy_considerations: Authority of the court exists for advancement of justice and if any attempt is made to abuse that authority so as to produce injustice, the court has power to prevent such abuse. It would be an abuse of the process of the court to allow any action which would result in injustice and prevent promotion of justice.

Criminal antecedents of the accused cannot be the sole consideration to decline to quash the criminal proceedings – An accused has a legitimate right to say before the Court that howsoever bad his antecedents may be, still if the FIR fails to disclose commission of any oﬀence then the court should not decline to quash the criminal case.

Initiation of prosecution has adverse and harsh consequence for the persons named as accused – Thus, the requirement and need to balance the law enforcement power and protection of citizens from injustice and harassment must be maintained – State owes a duty to ensure that no crime goes unpunished as also owes a duty to ensure that none of its subjects are unnecessarily harassed.
